title: Infra GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts & CI/CD Consolidated Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Consolidated infrastructure engineering playbook covering GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking guardrails, Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD best practices, and operational runbooks for day-2 ops.
content:
Overview
--------
This playbook consolidates guidance and operational runbooks for Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering focused on our GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud account structure and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD pipelines. Intended audience: infra engineers, SREs, platform engineers, and on-call responders. This is a production-grade reference (not a design brainstorm).

Scope
-----
- GPU fleet sizing and lifecycle (provisioning, decommissioning, pod sizing)
- Central cloud account structure and networking guardrails (VPCs, subnets, egress, peering)
- Approved Terraform/IaC modules and patterns for GPU nodes, autoscaling, and networking
- CI/CD pipelines for infra and model-serving runtime (build, test, canary, apply)
- Runbooks for common incidents and day-2 operations

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity team (engineering)
- Secondary owners: infra/networking, infra-ci-cd teams
- Oncall escalation: see Oncall and escalation section; contact rotation lives in PagerDuty (service: infra.ops.gpu)

Capacity targets & SLOs
-----------------------
- Target utilization for general-purpose pools: 65% to 75% steady-state
- Peak buffer: maintain 20% spare capacity to cover burst workloads and failover
- Cold-start SLO: 95% of provisioning operations complete within 6 minutes (measured from request to GPU-ready node in the cluster)
- Request-level latency SLO (serving runtime): p95 < 120ms for short completions, p99 < 500ms (routing/edge only)
- Cost SLO: $/token target improvements tracked per quarter; infra team provides recommendations during capacity reviews

GPU fleet architecture (summary)
--------------------------------
- Pools: split by instance family and workload type
  - gp-prod-xlarge: low-latency serving (pinned model variants)
  - gp-batch-large: throughput-heavy batch workloads (auto-scaling enabled)
  - gp-dev-shared: dev/test workloads (preemptible/spot allowed)
- Control plane: Kubernetes (EKS/GKE) with node pools backed by autoscaling groups and cluster-autoscaler + Karpenter where supported
- Disk: ephemeral NVMe for inference cache; persistent EBS/EFS for model artifacts when required
- Quota tracking: cloud-accounts/quotas service exports daily metrics to datadog; alert if available GPUs < 25% of target capacity

Cloud accounts & networking guardrails
------------------------------------
- Account topology:
  - org-root: billing and org policies
  - infra-shared: CI/CD runners, terraform state backends, central logging, IAM automation
  - prod-<region>: production workloads per region (tight egress rules, private control plane endpoints)
  - dev-<team>: sandbox accounts with quotas and strict cost controls
- Networking:
  - All production clusters must use private cluster endpoints and no public kubeapi access
  - VPC design: three availability zones, dedicated subnets for GPU nodepools, ingress via ALB/NLB in separate public subnets, NAT gateways in each AZ for outbound egress
  - Egress policies: use proxy-egress for third-party calls; deny wide-open 0.0.0.0/0 egress from pod CIDR by default
  - Peering and transit: centralized transit gateway for cross-account connectivity; restrict peering to explicit CIDR lists defined in terraform variables

Terraform / IaC module patterns
------------------------------
- Module registry: internal terraform registry host: registry.redwood-infra.internal (docs in infra-team wiki)
- Approved modules: gpu-nodepool, cluster-autoscaler, vpc-core, vpc-peering, iam-service-roles, s3-artifact-bucket, kms-key-rotation
- Patterns and constraints:
  - All modules must be parameterized (cidr, azs, tags, instance_types, spot_percentage) and include example usage and tests (unit + plan-only integration)
  - State management: remote state in S3 + DynamoDB locking for AWS; backend config standardized in infra-shared account
  - Secrets: never hard-code secrets in tfvars; use SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager + kms-key referencing
  - Drift detection: run terraform plan in CI nightly for critical envs and open PRs for diffs exceeding threshold (see CI/CD section)

CI/CD and build pipelines
------------------------
- Repositories: infra modules live in git (gitlab/github) under org: redwood-infra/modules/
- Pipeline stages (recommended pattern):
  1. lint (tflint, tfsec rules)
  2. unit test (terragrunt/terratest mocks where applicable)
  3. plan (with -out plan.tfplan) against a sandbox account using ephemeral credentials
  4. policy checks (OPA/Gatekeeper / policy-as-code)
  5. apply (manual approval for prod) OR merge-triggered apply for dev accounts
- Canary strategy for infra changes: incremental rollout across accounts/regions via staged workspaces:
  - Stage 1: infra-shared sandbox (dev-001)
  - Stage 2: non-prod region (staging)
  - Stage 3: prod-secondary region (one region)
  - Stage 4: all prod regions (automated but monitored)
- CI secrets: stored in vault (HashiCorp Vault) with dynamic credentials for each pipeline run

Runbooks and playbooks (day-2 ops)
----------------------------------
1) GPU node degraded / OOM errors
- Symptoms: elevated OOMKilled pods, model-serving crashes, p95 latency spike > 2x baseline
- Owner: infra/gpu-capacity
- Steps:
  1. Check cluster node status: kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=gpu
  2. Identify defective node: kubectl describe node <node> and check dmesg/kernel logs via journalctl (ssh to node if necessary)
  3. Cordon and drain: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  4. If underlying hardware fault: mark for reprovision in inventory and trigger replacement runbook (see appendix)
  5. Monitor pods rescheduled; scale up a recovery nodepool if autoscaler didn't react within 5m

2) Cluster out-of-capacity (scale failure)
- Symptoms: pending pods with reason InsufficientGPU or InsufficientResources
- Owner: infra/gpu-capacity / infra-sre
- Steps:
  1. Check pending pods and reason: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
  2. Confirm autoscaler activity: check cluster-autoscaler logs and AWS ASG activity (or Karpenter events)
  3. If autoscaler unhealthy: restart autoscaler controller pod and inspect IAM permissions used by ASG role
  4. Emergency manual scale: increase nodepool desired count via terraform-backed variable in infra-shared workspace and trigger a CI apply for prod emergency (follow emergency change approval in infra runbooks)
  5. Post-incident: open a postmortem if incident duration > 15 minutes or customer impact observed

Monitoring, dashboards and alerts
--------------------------------
- Dashboards (Datadog):
  - GPU Fleet Overview: available GPUs, utilization, memory pressure, spot eviction rate
  - Autoscaler Health: queue depth, scale events, failed scale attempts
  - Networking: packet drops, NAT gateway egress errors, VPC flow anomalies
- Key alerts (examples):
  - available_gpus_percent < 25% for 5m -> PagerDuty P1 to infra.ops.gpu
  - cluster_autoscaler_failures > 3 in 10m -> P1 to infra-sre
  - spot_eviction_rate > 8% in gp-dev-shared -> P2 to infra-gpu-capacity
  - terraform_plan_drift_detected (critical changes) -> P1 to infra-ci-cd and owner team

Operational procedures and runbook hygiene
-----------------------------------------
- Review cadence: capacity review every 2 weeks; quarterly architecture review for fleet mix and instance families
- Maintenance windows: schedule monthly maintenance windows per region (announce 72h in advance via status.redwood.com)
- Runbook ownership: runbooks must include owner, last run, and test checklist; validate runbooks in game-days twice per year

Change management and rollout steps (example: nodepool instance type upgrade)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Prepare: update module example and run terraform plan in sandbox (include canary tags)
2. CI: run full pipeline (lint -> test -> plan -> policy) and submit merge request
3. Canary: apply to staging and monitor node/serving metrics for 4 hours
4. Gradual rollout: update one prod region, monitor for 24h; if no regressions, roll remaining regions in parallel batches of 2
5. Rollback plan: maintain previous instance profile in module variables; if regressions detected, restore previous desired count and instance_type and reapply

Appendix: module usage examples
------------------------------
- gpu-nodepool example (tf snippet):
  module "gp_prod_xlarge" {
    source = "registry.redwood-infra.internal/gpu-nodepool/aws"
    name = "gp-prod-xlarge"
    instance_types = ["g5.12xlarge", "g5.8xlarge"]
    desired_capacity = 40
    min_capacity = 30
    max_capacity = 60
    spot_percentage = 10
    tags = { team = "model-serving", env = "prod" }
  }

- vpc-core example (tfvars table):
  - name: prod-us-west-2
  - azs: ["us-west-2a","us-west-2b","us-west-2c"]
  - pod_cidr: 10.20.0.0/16
  - public_subnet_cidrs: ["10.20.0.0/24","10.20.1.0/24","10.20.2.0/24"]
  - private_subnet_cidrs: ["10.20.10.0/24","10.20.11.0/24","10.20.12.0/24"]
